verdicts.reason: The user at CLIENT01 starts the connection by FQDN rdp01.1sn0s.lab, which is the name later matched against the SAN (F-01). The client owns no server certificate.
An amber pending pulse travels on a network channel (transport network). Nothing is trusted yet, and the channel is not used as a trust link.
The server's listener lights up, and the server is shown as the party that needs an identity (F-01).

The card is shown as signed by its own separate key (KEY-RDP-SELF-PRIV): not unsigned, and with no trusted issuer (F-02). The EKU is Server Authentication and the store is Remote Desktop, both correct. Nothing is accepted, and the attempt closes (E-02.2c). Kerberos-scope documentation nit in PKI-S0R2-06.

Group Policy names RDPAuth on the server, and enrollment is driven by server-side policy processing. No client connection is pending (the channel is dark). The badge stands for the template name only; no key or certificate comes from AD.
A new key pair (KP-RDP, separate from KP-RDP-SELF) is generated locally in a machine key container. The notes say the template definition is read before key generation (F-03, F-05).
The private key is stored locally with transport local, has a distinct lock-motif shape and is anchored (F-03).

REQ-RDP holds KEY-RDP-PUB and request information, in the format 'PKCS #10 inside CMC'. contains_private_key is false and subject_in_request is null, which is consistent with build-from-AD (F-04, F-07).
Proof of possession uses KEY-RDP-PRIV with local transport. The beam is light from the container, no key-shaped object moves, and the CA verifies the signature in check 4 (F-03, F-04).

A separate query pulse goes to AD and back. Enrollment Services objects show that only ISSUING_CA1 publishes TPL-RDPAUTH. The capsule stays at the outbound port, and AD never receives, signs or forwards the request (F-05, AR-04, AR-05).
The request is submitted over the network only to the eligible, publishing CA (ISSUING_CA1), along a route clear of AD. It never touches the root.

All four F-06 checks appear in order: authentication, publication, Enroll plus Request Certificates, and template policy including proof-of-possession verification. The subject is built from the AD computer object (F-07).

The request is consumed at the CA. KEY-CA1-PRIV stays in its module and drives the press. CERT-RDP has SAN rdp01.1sn0s.lab, EKU 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.54.1.2, CA=false, and AIA/CDP pointing to Issuing CA 1's objects on pki.1sn0s.lab (F-08, AR-06).
The certificate returns and is installed in LocalMachine\My beside the private key, which has not moved (F-09). The intermediate certificate copy is not delivered here; see PKI-S0R2-01.

The root is offline (online false, network_connected false) and cable-free. Its self-seal is revealed with transport none and uses_key null, and its key module and press stay dark. Trust anchor status is attributed to installation, not to being self-signed (AR-01, F-17).

The scene is in the flashback era. The subordinate-CA request is signed with KEY-CA1-PRIV, carried on offline media and consumed at the root. The root signs CERT-CA1 (CA=true) with KEY-ROOT-PRIV, and the certificate is carried back. No end-entity request appears (AR-02). Wording nit in the frozen docs ('the request is signed offline'): see PKI-S0R2-04.
The issuer link has transport logical, so it is a trust link, not a cable. 'Trust anchor' is used only for the root, and Issuing CA 1 is trusted only through the chain (AR-03, F-15, F-17).

This is a new connection attempt (E-06.1a). The server sends CERT-RDP plus CERT-CA1 and no root certificate. The handshake signature uses KEY-RDP-PRIV locally, and only the signature impression travels (F-10, F-03). Nits: the intermediate's origin on the server (PKI-S0R2-01) and the client-side verification of the proof (PKI-S0R2-03).

The chain docks to a root already in the Trusted Root store (installed_before_film true). The recall has transport none and era recall. Chain building is not presented as proof of identity; the name check stays separate (F-11).

AIA is conditional with transport none and trust_source false. Nothing is fetched, because the intermediate was presented. The tag says fetching never creates trust (F-11, AR-06). The kiosk 'answers' wording is a nit: see PKI-S0R2-09.

The checks are distinct. The name match against the SAN dNSName is its own identity check. Basic Constraints and critical extensions are folded into check 1 in the notes. The EKU check accepts RDA or Server Authentication, and revocation stays pending (F-12, F-08).

There is one CRL fetch per non-root link: CRL-CA1 for CERT-RDP and CRL-ROOT for CERT-CA1. The root is not checked. OCSP is conditional and not deployed. The tick resolves after both fetches end (65.6 then 65.8). The OCSP host modelling is a nit: see PKI-S0R2-08.
Green appears on the new connection only after every check has resolved (E-06.6a at 67.2, after E-06.5d ends at 66.6).
WEB01 serves portal.1sn0s.lab. The template is chosen by an authorized request, not by autoenrollment, which is correct for a subject-in-request template (F-07, F-14).
The key pair is generated locally and the private key is anchored. REQ-WEB carries the subject and SAN, is signed with KEY-WEB-PRIV and contains no private key (F-03, F-04, F-07).
Both CAs are considered and only ISSUING_CA2 is eligible. Issuing CA 1 turns grey with the 'not published here' tag. The query goes to AD while the request is held at the port (F-05, F-14, AR-04).
The request goes only to ISSUING_CA2, clear of AD, Issuing CA 1 and the root.
The same four checks run. The restricted-Enroll note is attached to the Enroll check, which is correct reasoning for a supply-in-request template (F-06, F-07).

The request is consumed and KEY-CA2-PRIV signs in place. CERT-WEB has SAN portal.1sn0s.lab, Server Authentication EKU and CA=false, and is installed in LocalMachine\My beside the existing key (F-03, F-08, F-09).

The issuer link has transport logical and both paths end at the same root (F-15). Nothing in the model makes the root act. A staging nit about CERT-CA2 appearing only after CA 2 has already signed: see PKI-S0R2-05.

The server sends CERT-WEB and CERT-CA2 and proves possession with KEY-WEB-PRIV. The chain goes to the same pre-installed root. CRL-CA2 covers CERT-WEB and CRL-ROOT covers CERT-CA2, with no root check. Green appears last. Event-ordering nits in PKI-S0R2-02; browser revocation-default nit in PKI-S0R2-07.
Two trust paths (transport logical) converge at one root. The root stays cable-free, and 'trusted root' and 'trust anchor' are used only for the root (F-14, F-15, F-17).
The title card makes no PKI claim that could contradict F-15.

findings.evidence: E-06.1c presents CERT-CA1 from RDP_SERVER, and the storyboard says Issuing CA 1's card 'lift[s] from the chassis'. But no event ever puts a copy of CERT-CA1 on RDP_SERVER: E-04.5a returns only CERT-RDP, and CERT-CA1's only store is 'CA database and CA certificate store' on the CA, also shown on Issuing CA 1's crown. The same gap exists for CERT-CA2 on WEB_SERVER (E-09.1c, with only CERT-WEB returned in E-08.2c).
findings.why: The server can send the intermediate only if it holds a copy, normally received with the enrollment response chain or placed in its Intermediate Certification Authorities store. As modelled, the intermediate card either appears from nowhere on the server or is the same object as the CA's crown card. An ADCS engineer would ask where the server got it.
findings.direction: Give the server a modelled copy of the issuing CA certificate before presentation. For example, the enrollment response in B-04.5 and B-08.2 returns the end-entity certificate together with the issuing CA certificate, which goes into the server's Intermediate store. Say so in the notes for B-04.5 and B-08.2, and keep it distinct from the CA's own crown certificate.

findings.evidence: E-09.1b (present_cert CERT-WEB) starts at 93.4 s, before the client's connection pulse E-09.1a has reached WEB01 at 93.6 s. E-09.1o (the revocation validation_check) starts at 96.6 s, the same instant the first CRL fetch E-09.1m starts and before E-09.1n (96.7-97.1 s) completes. In B-06.5, by contrast, E-06.5d starts at 65.8 s, after both fetches end at 65.6 s.
findings.why: The server cannot present its certificate before the client's connection arrives. A revocation tick that starts resolving before the CRLs are in hand suggests revocation passed without the CRLs. These overlaps are small, but they invert causal order in the model.
findings.direction: Order the B-09.1 events causally: present_cert begins at or after the pulse arrives, and the revocation check begins after the last CRL fetch lands, as in B-06.5. Add a model integrity test that these events do not overlap.

findings.evidence: HS-RDP travels to the client (E-06.1e), and the notes say 'The client verifies that signature with the certificate's public key'. But no event depicts that verification, and the notes define tick 2 ('Signatures verify') as certificate signatures only. On screen, nothing specifies what happens to the handshake proof after it arrives. HS-WEB in B-09.1 has the same gap.
findings.why: F-10 says a certificate alone proves nothing; possession proven by a verified signature is what binds the connection. If the proof arrives and nothing checks it, the viewer sees decoration rather than a verified binding.
findings.direction: Show the handshake-proof impression being matched or verified against the server certificate's public key on arrival (in B-06.1 or as part of B-06.2), and state which visual covers it in the notes. Give HS-RDP and HS-WEB a defined end of life.

findings.evidence: The spec B-05.2 says of Issuing CA 1's request: 'It is signed offline and carried back.' The glossary entry 'Offline root ceremony' says 'The root signs the request'. The notes' on-screen line and the model summary repeat 'is signed offline' for the request. The events are correct: E-05.2c consumes REQ-CA1, E-05.2d signs CERT-CA1, and E-05.2e carries CERT-CA1 back.
findings.why: A CA does not sign a request. The request was already signed by its requester (proof of possession, F-04), and the root issues and signs a certificate. This mix-up of request and certificate is exactly the confusion the film exists to prevent, and it sits in frozen terminology (L-08).
findings.direction: By Chief of Staff amendment, reword to say the root issues and signs Issuing CA 1's CA certificate from the request, and that the certificate is carried back. Align the glossary, the notes and the model summary.

findings.evidence: The storyboard says 'Issuing CA 2's own certificate lights on its vault crown, and a gold-to-violet trust link grows from the same root down to it'. This happens right after Issuing CA 2 has already signed CERT-WEB (B-08.2). Unlike CERT-CA1, there is no flashback and no on-screen cue that CERT-CA2 already existed. B-07.3 does not establish CERT-CA2 on the crown either.
findings.why: A CA certificate that appears for the first time in the present, with a link growing out of the root, can read as the root issuing it now, and as Issuing CA 2 signing before it was certified. The B-05.1 constraint (the root performs no operation in the present) should visibly hold here too.
findings.direction: Establish CERT-CA2 already present, dimmed, on Issuing CA 2's crown when the vault first appears (B-07.3), and make B-08.3 a reveal sweep only. Explicitly keep the root's key module and press dark in B-08.3 and B-09.2, and say in the storyboard that the link is a reveal of an existing issuer relationship.

findings.evidence: The lab as modelled is exactly the F-16 Kerberos case: domain-joined CLIENT01, domain-joined RDP01, connecting by FQDN rdp01.1sn0s.lab, with NLA described in the notes for B-01.1 and B-06.6. Yet the notes for B-02.2 say the Remote Desktop client 'warns ... depending on its server-authentication setting'. The scope section offers 'policy requires a trusted certificate' as a condition but names no concrete policy.
findings.why: In the configuration the film shows, Kerberos via CredSSP would normally authenticate the server, and mstsc would not warn about the self-signed certificate. The notes should not imply the warning is the normal outcome here, and the 'policy requires' condition should be backed by a named setting or removed.
findings.direction: In the notes, state plainly that in this lab configuration Kerberos would usually satisfy server authentication. Explain that the 'Unverified' tag means the certificate cannot be validated through the PKI, and that a warning appears where Kerberos server authentication is unavailable (IP address, non-domain name or non-domain client). Name the specific policy if 'policy requires a trusted certificate' is kept.

findings.evidence: The notes for B-09.1 describe 'The browser on CLIENT01' fetching one CRL per non-root link, with no caveat about browser behaviour.
findings.why: Chromium-based browsers (Edge, Chrome) do not perform online CRL/OCSP revocation checks by default, and Firefox does not consume CDP CRLs. Online checking for locally installed anchors is enabled by enterprise policy (for example RequireOnlineRevocationChecksForLocalAnchors). An ADCS engineer would add this caveat. The RDP client (CryptoAPI-based) does check revocation by default.
findings.direction: Add a docs-only note to B-09.1 that browser revocation checking depends on the client and on policy, and that the film depicts a client configured to check CDP/CRL per link (consistent with F-13). The on-screen beat does not need to change.

findings.evidence: SVC-OCSP is modelled with host PKI_HTTP although deployed is false, and the 'OCSP if deployed' tag is attached to SVC-OCSP.
findings.why: No Online Responder exists in this lab (AR-07). Giving the non-existent responder a host, and anchoring its tag there, risks placing the tag at the pki.1sn0s.lab kiosk, which would imply that a responder lives at the publication point.
findings.direction: Model the undeployed responder with no host, and anchor the 'OCSP if deployed' tag to the client's revocation check slot, not to the kiosk.

findings.evidence: The storyboard says 'the distant pki.1sn0s.lab kiosk answers with a faint light. Nothing travels.'
findings.why: An 'answer' from the publication point implies a request and response took place, which contradicts 'nothing is fetched here'. It also gives the AIA location an active, responding role, the opposite of 'never a trust source'.
findings.direction: Have the kiosk only indicated as the location where the issuer certificate could be fetched (a passive highlight tied to the card's AIA port), with no response cue.
